title: Job 30:16–31
context: Job continues his lament, turning from the mockers to his own body and to God. His soul is poured out, his bones are pierced at night, and his pains give no rest (30:16–18). He says that God has cast him into the mire, so that he has become like dust and ashes (30:19). He then speaks to God directly: “I cry to you, and you do not answer me” (30:20), and “You have turned to be cruel to me” (30:21). He expects that God will bring him to death, “to the house appointed for all living” (30:23). The meaning of 30:24 is uncertain in Hebrew, and translations differ; this page reads it as Job asking whether a person in calamity may not reach out and cry for help. Job recalls that he himself wept for the troubled and grieved for the needy (30:25), yet when he looked for good, evil came (30:26). He ends in mourning, a companion of jackals and ostriches, his skin blackened and his harp turned to weeping (30:27–31). Both traditions read these words as honest lament brought before God, neither endorsed as doctrine nor condemned as unbelief, and both let the LORD’s later answer and verdict (42:7) do their own work.

verses.text: “Now my soul is poured out within me. Days of affliction have taken hold of me.
verses.arminianNotes: “Now my soul is poured out within me.” Arminian readers hear the depth of Job’s exhaustion and grief. His inner life feels drained, and days of affliction have taken hold of him without relief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear honest anguish of soul. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with pastoral care, recognizing that suffering can leave a person feeling emptied, and both affirm that such grief may be spoken before God.

verses.text: In the night season my bones are pierced in me, and the pains that gnaw me take no rest.
verses.arminianNotes: In the night his bones are pierced and his pains give no rest. Arminian readers note the physical reality of Job’s suffering. Night brings no relief, and his pain is constant, a detail that should shape how his words are heard.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the bodily affliction described in the prologue (2:7) continuing. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with compassion and recognize that physical pain deeply affects a sufferer’s speech.

verses.text: My garment is disfigured by great force. It binds me about as the collar of my tunic.
verses.arminianNotes: Job’s garment is disfigured and binds him like the collar of his tunic. Arminian readers note that the image is difficult, perhaps describing his clothing clinging to his diseased body. They hold its exact sense loosely.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the uncertain sense of the lines while hearing Job’s distress. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of his lament over bodily suffering, and neither presses a precise interpretation.

verses.text: He has cast me into the mire. I have become like dust and ashes.
verses.arminianNotes: “He has cast me into the mire. I have become like dust and ashes.” Arminian readers note that Job attributes his humiliation to God. They hear it as the honest perception of a sufferer, offered in lament rather than as a doctrinal claim.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear Job tracing his condition to God. Shared ground: both traditions note that “dust and ashes” returns in Job’s later words at 42:6, a line whose sense is itself read in more than one way, and both read this verse as lament without resolving its relation to that later moment.

verses.text: I cry to you, and you do not answer me. I stand up, and you gaze at me.
verses.arminianNotes: “I cry to you, and you do not answer me.” Arminian readers hear the pain of unanswered prayer. Job keeps speaking to God even when he senses no reply, which is itself an act of continued relationship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear honest lament addressed to God and recall that God does answer Job later in the book. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse pastorally, affirming that believers may bring the experience of God’s silence to God.

verses.text: You have turned to be cruel to me. With the might of your hand you persecute me.
verses.arminianNotes: “You have turned to be cruel to me.” Arminian readers hear raw anguish. They do not endorse the accusation as true of God, nor do they condemn Job for voicing it; they hear the cry of a man who cannot see the whole story.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear lament rather than settled doctrine, and remember the prologue the reader can see but Job cannot. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse pastorally, neither endorsing nor condemning it, and let 42:7 do its own work.

verses.text: You lift me up to the wind, and drive me with it. You dissolve me in the storm.
verses.arminianNotes: God lifts Job to the wind and dissolves him in the storm. Arminian readers note the images of powerlessness. Job feels tossed about by forces he cannot resist, and he attributes this to God in the language of lament.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear honest anguish in the images of wind and storm. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetry of distress, reported soberly and pastorally, without treating it as a doctrinal account of God’s ways.

verses.text: For I know that you will bring me to death, to the house appointed for all living.
verses.arminianNotes: Job expects God to bring him “to the house appointed for all living.” Arminian readers note that Job sees death as near. His lament includes the expectation that his suffering will end only in the grave.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear Job’s expectation of death and note the reminder that death is appointed for all. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with compassion and note that the book’s ending will surprise Job’s expectation (42:10–17).

verses.text: “However doesn’t one stretch out a hand in his fall? Or in his calamity therefore cry for help?
verses.arminianNotes: “However doesn’t one stretch out a hand in his fall?” Arminian readers note that this verse is uncertain in Hebrew. A likely sense is that anyone in calamity reaches out and cries for help, as Job is doing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the difficulty of the verse and read it cautiously. Shared ground: both traditions take it as Job defending his cry for help, and both decline to build conclusions on an obscure line.

verses.text: Didn’t I weep for him who was in trouble? Wasn’t my soul grieved for the needy?
verses.arminianNotes: “Didn’t I weep for him who was in trouble?” Arminian readers note Job’s appeal to his own compassion. He wept for others in distress, yet now no one weeps for him, which adds to his sense of injustice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the verse as echoing 29:12–17 and standing against Eliphaz’s charges (22:5–9). Shared ground: both traditions read it as part of Job’s defense, without harmonizing it with the friends’ accusations.

verses.text: When I looked for good, then evil came. When I waited for light, darkness came.
verses.arminianNotes: “When I looked for good, then evil came.” Arminian readers hear the bewilderment of a man whose expectations have been overturned. Job had trusted that righteousness would bring good, and instead he met calamity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear honest perplexity at suffering that seems undeserved. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with compassion and see in it a question the book takes seriously rather than answering quickly.

verses.text: My heart is troubled, and doesn’t rest. Days of affliction have come on me.
verses.arminianNotes: Job’s heart is troubled and does not rest; days of affliction have come on him. Arminian readers note the restlessness of his inner life. His suffering is not only physical but emotional and spiritual.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the deep turmoil of a troubled heart. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse pastorally, recognizing that the faithful may experience prolonged inner distress, and both treat it as honest lament.

verses.text: I go mourning without the sun. I stand up in the assembly, and cry for help.
verses.arminianNotes: Job goes mourning without the sun and cries for help in the assembly. Arminian readers note the contrast with 29:7, where he once sat honored at the gate. Now he stands in public only to cry for help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the painful reversal of Job’s public role. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Job’s lament, and both see in it the depth of his fall from honor to helplessness.

verses.text: I am a brother to jackals, and a companion to ostriches.
verses.arminianNotes: “I am a brother to jackals, and a companion to ostriches.” Arminian readers note the images of desolation. Job feels so isolated that his only companions seem to be creatures of the wilderness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the images as poetry of loneliness and mourning. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as lament, and both note how Job, who once sat among nobles, now feels he belongs among wild creatures.

verses.text: My skin grows black and peels from me. My bones are burned with heat.
verses.arminianNotes: Job’s skin grows black and peels, and his bones burn with heat. Arminian readers note the vivid description of his illness. The physical suffering introduced in the prologue (2:7) continues to weigh on him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the bodily reality of Job’s affliction. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with compassion, recognizing the toll of long illness, and both report its details soberly without expanding them.

verses.text: Therefore my harp has turned to mourning, and my pipe into the voice of those who weep.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore my harp has turned to mourning.” Arminian readers note the closing image of joy turned to grief. Instruments once used for celebration now sound only lament, a fitting end to Job’s description of his present state.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the end of Job’s lament before his oath of clearance in chapter 31. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse pastorally and see it as preparing for Job’s final appeal (31:35).
